### 8.1 Wave-Particle Energies

Light exhibits both wave and particle properties, a concept known as wave-particle duality. Let's explore these fascinating properties:

#### Electromagnetic Waves and Photons
- Light travels as electromagnetic waves with electric and magnetic fields
- These waves can also behave as discrete particles called photons
- Each photon carries a specific amount of energy

#### Wave-Particle Duality
- Light demonstrates wave properties like diffraction and interference
- In certain experiments, light acts as particles (photons)
- Einstein used this duality to explain the photoelectric effect

#### Energy Quantization 
- Energy of electromagnetic radiation comes in discrete packets
- Energy (E) of a photon relates to frequency (f): E = hf
- Higher frequencies mean higher energy photons

#### Planck's Constant and Photoelectric Effect
- Planck's constant (h) ≈ 6.626 × 10^-34 J·s
- Photoelectric effect: light hits metal, electrons are ejected
- Only photons above threshold frequency can eject electrons
- Einstein won Nobel Prize for explaining this phenomenon

**Key Equations:**
- E = hf (photon energy)
- λf = c (wave equation)
- KEmax = hf - φ (photoelectric effect)

### 8.2 Electric Charges and Fields

#### Fundamental Concepts
- Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter
- Two types: positive and negative charges
- Like charges repel, opposite charges attract
- Charge is conserved in isolated systems

#### Coulomb's Law
- Describes force between charged particles
- Force proportional to product of charges
- Inversely proportional to distance squared
- F = k(q₁q₂)/r²
- k is Coulomb's constant ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N⋅m²/C²

#### Electric Fields
- Region where electric forces act
- Field lines show direction of force
- Field strength proportional to line density
- Points from positive to negative charge
- E = F/q defines field strength

#### Gauss's Law
- Relates electric flux to enclosed charge
- Flux through closed surface
- ∮E⋅dA = Q/ε₀
- Useful for symmetric charge distributions

#### Electric Potential
- Work done per unit charge
- Potential difference creates electric fields
- Measured in volts (V)
- V = W/q relationship
- Conservative force field property

### 8.3 Electromagnetic Power and Energy

#### Electromagnetic Induction
- Moving magnets create electric fields
- Changing magnetic fields induce current flow
- Faraday's law: EMF = -N(ΔΦ/Δt)
- Lenz's law determines current direction

#### Power Transmission
- Electric power = voltage × current
- Power loss in transmission lines
- Step-up transformers increase voltage
- High voltage reduces current and power loss
- P = I²R relationship for power loss

#### Energy in Fields
- Both electric and magnetic fields store energy
- Electric field energy: UE = ½CV²
- Magnetic field energy: UB = ½LI²
- Energy density proportional to field strength squared

#### Maxwell's Equations
- Four fundamental equations
- Describe all electromagnetic phenomena
- Predict electromagnetic waves
- Unify electricity and magnetism
- Lead to wave equation c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀)

**Key Equations:**
- P = VI (power)
- EMF = -N(ΔΦ/Δt) (Faraday's law)
- P = I²R (power loss)

## Unit 9 | Electricity

### 9.1 Electrostatics

#### Static Electricity Fundamentals
- Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter
- Objects can become charged by friction or contact
- Charge transfer occurs between materials
- Conductors allow charge flow, insulators restrict it

#### Charge Distribution
- Like charges repel, opposite charges attract
- Charges redistribute to minimize potential energy
- Conductors hold charge on surface
- Sharp points concentrate charge (lightning rods)
- Charge density varies with surface geometry

#### Electric Potential Difference
- Potential difference measured in volts
- Work per unit charge between points
- Higher potential to lower potential flow
- Earth typically used as reference (ground)
- Electric field lines perpendicular to equipotential surfaces

#### Capacitance
- Ability to store electric charge
- Measured in farads (F)
- C = Q/V relationship
- Parallel plate capacitor basics
- Energy storage: U = ½CV²
- Common applications in electronics

**Key Equations:**
- C = Q/V (capacitance)
- E = F/q (electric field)
- V = W/q (potential difference)
### 9.2 Electric Circuits

#### Current and Voltage
- Electric current is the flow of charge through a conductor
- Current (I) measured in amperes (A)
- Voltage (V) is electric potential difference
- Conventional current flows from positive to negative
- Current density depends on conductor cross-section

#### Series and Parallel Circuits
- Series: components connected end-to-end
    - Same current through all components
    - Voltage divides across components
    - Total resistance: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂ + R₃
- Parallel: components connected across same points
    - Same voltage across components
    - Current divides through branches
    - Total resistance: 1/Rtotal = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃

#### Resistance and Ohm's Law
- Resistance (R) opposes current flow
- Measured in ohms (Ω)
- Ohm's law: V = IR
- Temperature affects resistance
- Resistivity depends on material properties

#### Kirchhoff's Laws
- Current law (KCL): sum of currents at junction = 0
- Voltage law (KVL): sum of voltages around loop = 0
- Used to analyze complex circuits
- Conservation of charge and energy principles

#### Power and Energy
- Electric power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R
- Energy transferred: E = Pt
- Power measured in watts (W)
- Energy measured in joules (J)
- Heat generation in resistors

**Key Equations:**
- V = IR (Ohm's law)
- P = VI (power)
- Series resistance: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂ + R₃
- Parallel resistance: 1/Rtotal = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃

## Unit 10 | Optics

### 10.1 Geometric Optics

#### Reflection and Refraction
- Light rays travel in straight lines
- Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
- Refraction occurs when light changes medium
- Snell's law: n₁sin(θ₁) = n₂sin(θ₂)
- Total internal reflection when angle exceeds critical angle

#### Mirrors
- Plane mirrors form virtual images
- Curved mirrors: concave and convex
- Focal point where parallel rays converge
- Mirror equation: 1/f = 1/p + 1/i
- Ray diagrams show image formation

#### Lenses
- Converging (convex) focuses light
- Diverging (concave) spreads light
- Focal length depends on curvature
- Lens equation: 1/f = 1/p + 1/i
- Magnification: m = -i/p

#### Optical Instruments
- Human eye uses lens and retina
- Microscopes magnify tiny objects
- Telescopes gather distant light
- Cameras focus light on sensors
- Fiber optics use total internal reflection

**Key Equations:**
- n₁sin(θ₁) = n₂sin(θ₂) (Snell's law)
- 1/f = 1/p + 1/i (mirror/lens equation)
- m = -i/p (magnification)

### 10.2 Wave Optics

#### Wave Nature of Light
- Light propagates as electromagnetic waves
- Wavelengths of visible light: 380-700 nanometers
- Each color has distinct wavelength
- White light contains all visible wavelengths
- Speed of light in vacuum: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s

#### Interference
- Waves combine through superposition
- Constructive interference: waves add together
- Destructive interference: waves cancel out
- Double-slit experiment shows wave nature
- Thin film interference creates colorful patterns

#### Diffraction
- Light bends around obstacles
- Occurs through small openings
- Single-slit diffraction pattern
- Resolution limited by diffraction
- Diffraction gratings separate wavelengths

#### Polarization
- Light waves oscillate perpendicular to travel
- Polarizing filters select one oscillation direction
- Malus's law: I = I₀cos²θ
- LCD screens use polarization
- Polarized sunglasses reduce glare

**Key Equations:**
- c = λf (wave equation)
- d sin θ = mλ (diffraction grating)
- I = I₀cos²θ (Malus's law)
